payload.body: The submediant is scale degree 6 of a key: the pitch a major sixth above the tonic in a major key and a minor sixth above the tonic in a natural minor key, bearing the submediant function as the subordinate degree of the scale's upper region. In C major the submediant is A (the root of the iv chord, an A-minor triad), and in A natural minor it is F (the root of the VI chord, an F-major triad). Parameters: (1) intervallic status — the submediant sits a major sixth above the tonic in major keys and a minor sixth above the tonic in natural minor keys; it is a whole step above the dominant and a third below the tonic (a minor third in major keys, a major third in natural minor keys). (2) functional role — it is the degree that commonly moves to the dominant as a pre-dominant or colour degree (submediant–dominant motion, iv–V or VI–V), and it names the key a third from the tonic (the vi / VI key, one of the keys in mediant relation to the tonic). (3) relational definition — the submediant is defined relative to the tonic (the submediant of C major is A; of A minor is F) and is the sixth ordinal of the key's scale. Persistence mechanism: codified in Western tonal and harmonic theory, taught in music-theory and harmony curricula (scale-degree numbering; Roman-numeral analysis naming iv in major and VI in minor), reproduced in composition and analysis practice (identifying the submediant's pre-dominant motion and its role in modulation to the related key), and maintained through the conventions of tonal notation. It is distinguished from the mediant (scale degree 3 — a third above the tonic, the lower of the two 'mediant' degrees; the submediant is a sixth, not a third), from the dominant (scale degree 5 — the point of greatest harmonic tension; the submediant sits a whole step above it and bears a subordinate, preparatory function rather than the tension function), and from a bare pitch (any point on the pitch axis; the submediant is a pitch bearing a specific ordinal and function). [formal: submediantia | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

payload.scope: A human-made musical construct: the second scale degree of a key — the pitch a major second above the tonic in major keys, bearing the supertonic function as the degree of outward departure from the tonic into the pre-dominant region. Built to persist in Western tonal theory as the named second position of the diatonic scale.

payload.body: The supertonic is scale degree 2 of a key: the pitch a major second above the tonic (in a major key) or a minor second above the tonic (in a natural minor key), and the bearer of the supertonic function — the degree that moves from the tonic outward toward the pre-dominant region. In C major the supertonic is D (the root of the ii chord, a minor triad), and in A natural minor it is B (the root of the ii° chord, a diminished triad). PARAMETERS: (1) intervallic status — the supertonic sits a major second above the tonic in major keys and a minor second above the tonic in natural minor keys; it is a whole step below the mediant and a whole step above the tonic; (2) functional role — it commonly moves from the tonic to the pre-dominant region (tonic → supertonic → dominant motion, I–ii–V or I–vi–V), and in minor keys the supertonic triad is diminished (ii°) which gives it a leading quality of its own; (3) relational definition — the supertonic is defined relative to the tonic (the supertonic of C major is D; of A minor is B) and is the second ordinal of the key's scale. PERSISTENCE: codified in Western tonal and harmonic theory, taught in music-theory and harmony curricula (scale-degree numbering; Roman-numeral analysis naming ii in major and ii° in minor), reproduced in composition and analysis practice (identifying the supertonic's role in tonic-pre-dominant motion and in deceptive cadences where V resolves to vi — the supertonic's relative key), and maintained through the conventions of tonal notation. Distinctions: from the mediant (scale degree 3 — a third above the tonic, the degree between the tonic and the subdominant; the supertonic occupies the second, not the third, ordinal slot); from the tonic (scale degree 1 — the point of rest that the supertonic leaves; the supertonic is the first step of departure); from a bare pitch (any point on the pitch axis; the supertonic is a pitch bearing the specific second-degree status and the outward function); from the ii chord (the triad built on the second degree — a chord built ON the supertonic, not the degree and function itself). [formal: super-tertius | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

payload.body: The mediant is scale degree 3 of a key: the pitch a major third above the tonic (in a major key) or a minor third above the tonic (in a minor key), and the bearer of the mediant function — the degree that occupies the middle position of the diatonic scale and serves as the shared tone between the tonic and dominant functions. In C major the mediant is E (the root of the iii chord, a minor triad), and in A minor the mediant is C (the root of the I chord, a major triad). PARAMETERS: (1) intervallic status — the mediant sits a major third above the tonic in major keys and a minor third above the tonic in minor keys; it divides the perfect fifth (tonic to dominant) into two thirds, making it the harmonic midpoint of the diatonic fifth; (2) functional role — it is the degree that commonly functions as a weak pre-dominant (moving to the dominant as iii–V or to the tonic as iii–I), and it serves as the shared tone between the tonic triad (I) and the dominant triad (V): in C major, the mediant E is the third of the I chord and the seventh of the V chord, linking them; (3) relational definition — the mediant is defined relative to the tonic (the mediant of C major is E; of A minor is C) and is the third ordinal of the key's scale. PERSISTENCE: codified in Western tonal and harmonic theory, taught in music-theory and harmony curricula (scale-degree numbering; Roman-numeral analysis naming iii in major and I in minor), reproduced in composition and analysis practice (identifying the mediant's role in voice-leading, its function as a connecting degree between tonic and dominant areas), and maintained through the conventions of tonal notation. Distinctions: from the supertonic (scale degree 2 — a second above the tonic, the first degree of departure; the mediant occupies the third ordinal slot); from the subdominant (scale degree 4 — a fourth above the tonic, the degree of departure; the mediant is below the subdominant); from the dominant (scale degree 5 — the point of tension; the mediant sits a third below it and carries a subordinate role); from a bare pitch (any point on the pitch axis; the mediant is a pitch bearing the specific third-degree status and the middle-function); from the iii chord (the triad built on the third degree — a chord built ON the mediant, not the degree and function itself). The mediant is scale degree 3 of a key: the pitch a major third above the tonic (in a major key) or a minor third above the tonic (in a minor key), and the bearer of the mediant function — the degree that occupies the middle position of the diatonic scale and serves as the shared tone between the tonic and dominant functions. In C major the mediant is E (the root of the iii chord, a minor triad), and in A minor the mediant is C (the root of the I chord, a major triad). PARAMETERS: (1) intervallic status — the mediant sits a major third above the tonic in major keys and a minor third above the tonic in minor keys; it divides the perfect fifth (tonic to dominant) into two thirds, making it the harmonic midpoint of the diatonic fifth; (2) functional role — it is the degree that commonly functions as a weak pre-dominant (moving to the dominant as iii–V or to the tonic as iii–I), and it serves as the shared tone between the tonic triad (I) and the dominant triad (V): in C major, the mediant E is the third of the I chord and the seventh of the V chord, linking them; (3) relational definition — the mediant is defined relative to the tonic (the mediant of C major is E; of A minor is C) and is the third ordinal of the key's scale. payload.body: The mediant is scale degree 3 of a key: the pitch a major third above the tonic (in a major key) or a minor third above the tonic (in a minor key), and the bearer of the mediant function — the degree that occupies the middle position of the diatonic scale and divides the perfect fifth. In C major the mediant is E (the root of the iii chord, a minor triad), and in A minor the mediant is C (the root of the III chord, a major triad). PARAMETERS: (1) intervallic status — the mediant sits a major third above the tonic in major keys and a minor third above the tonic in minor keys; it divides the perfect fifth (tonic to dominant) into two thirds, making it the harmonic midpoint of the diatonic fifth; (2) functional role — it is the degree that commonly functions as a weak pre-dominant (moving to the dominant as iii–V or to the tonic as iii–I); the mediant triad (iii) is a standard pivot chord, sharing two tones with both the tonic triad and the dominant triad (in C major: I = C-E-G and iii = E-G-B share E and G; iii = E-G-B and V = G-B-D share G and B) — it is the chord, not the pitch, that links I and V, and the shared tone of the I and V triads themselves is G, the fifth degree, not the mediant; (3) relational definition — the mediant is defined relative to the tonic (the mediant of C major is E; of A minor is C) and is the third ordinal of the key's scale. PERSISTENCE: codified in Western tonal and harmonic theory, taught in music-theory and harmony curricula (scale-degree numbering; Roman-numeral analysis naming iii in major and III in minor), reproduced in composition and analysis practice (identifying the mediant's pre-dominant and pivot roles in voice-leading and modulation), and maintained through the conventions of tonal notation. Distinctions: from the supertonic (scale degree 2 — a second above the tonic, the first degree of departure; the mediant occupies the third ordinal slot); from the subdominant (scale degree 4 — a fourth above the tonic, the degree of departure; the mediant is below the subdominant); from the dominant (scale degree 5 — the point of tension; the mediant sits a third below it and carries a subordinate role); from a bare pitch (any point on the pitch axis; the mediant is a pitch bearing the specific third-degree status and the middle-function); from the iii chord (the triad built on the third degree — a chord built ON the mediant, not the degree and function itself). [formal: medius | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

payload.body: Infixation is a morphological process in which a language inserts a bound morpheme — an infix — into the interior of a word stem, splitting the stem into two parts that bracket the inserted element. Three parameters carve the construct: (1) the inserted material is a bound morpheme, not an independent word — this is what separates infixation from tmesis, which inserts a grammatically independent word into the same interior position; (2) the insertion occurs at a fixed morphophonological position within the stem (a specific boundary or segment), so the process is a rule of the grammar rather than a free choice of the speaker; (3) the host stem retains its lexical identity, and the infixed form remains analyzable as a variant of that stem. Paradigmatic cases: Tagalog actor-focus infix -um- (kain 'to eat' → k-um-in 'to eat'), and the frequently cited but disputed English -ab- (ab-sent, ab-sole). Infixation persists two ways: as a productive rule — speakers of a language coin new infixed forms on the fly, and the rule survives as long as it is applied — and as a stable category of description — grammars, morphology textbooks, and formal rule specifications continue to state where the infix attaches and what it marks. payload.body: Trousers are a human-made lower-body garment consisting of a waist section and two separate leg sections that descend from the waist, worn as a single unit covering both legs. Three parameters carve the construct: (1) bifurcated construction — two leg sections split at the crotch, in contrast to the single tube of a skirt; (2) leg coverage from the waist downward — full-length trousers carry each leg section to at least the ankle, and variants truncating the legs at the thigh are classified as shorts, an instance of this kind rather than a separate kind; (3) waist fastening — a waistband, drawstring, or closure, with a front fly or other closure. Trousers persist through garment manufacture: the two-legged cut, its tailoring and assembly conventions, and its standard position in dress codes and retail classification are reproduced by tailors and manufacturers and taught as a basic category of dress. [formal: bracae | substrate: matter | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

payload.name: tmesis
payload.scope: Tmesis is a human-made morphological operation — the process by which a grammatically independent word or phrase is inserted into the interior of a single lexical word — built to persist as a recognizable linguistic pattern in the languages that exhibit it and as a stable category of morphological description.
payload.sense: The morphological insertion of a free morpheme into a word stem, as opposed to the bound-morpheme insertion of infixation.
payload.distinction: The existing entry (if it exists) would need to be a different construct. Tmesis specifically involves grammatically independent (free) morphemes inserted into words, whereas any other sense of 'tmesis' would need to describe a genuinely different operation — one that does not involve splitting a single lexical word with material that has independent syntactic status. The boundness vs. freedom of the inserted element is the concrete distinction: tmesis uses free morphemes, everything else does not.

payload.body: Tmesis is a morphological operation in which a grammatically independent word or phrase — not a bound morpheme — is inserted into the interior of a single lexical word, splitting it into two parts that bracket the inserted element. Three parameters carve the construct: (1) the inserted material is a free morpheme with its own syntactic independence, distinguishing tmesis from infixation where the inserted material is a bound morpheme; (2) the host word retains its lexical identity and can be recovered by removing the inserted element, making the construction analyzable as a split original; (3) the insertion occurs at a conventionalized position within the host word's internal structure, typically between the first and second syllable or after a specific phoneme, rather than being freely insertable at any point. Paradigmatic cases: the English exclamatory tmesis "fan-frickin'-tastic" (fan + frickin' + tastic), the Greek tmesis in Homer ("κατὰ μοῦνον" split from a compound), and various Oceanic languages where interrogative particles are inserted into verbs. Tmesis persists through discourse convention: the split form becomes recognizable as a unit through repeated usage in expressive or emphatic contexts, and the phenomenon is catalogued in grammars of the languages that exhibit it. [formal: transfixio | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

payload.body: A suffix is a bound morpheme that attaches to the end of a word stem (or base), modifying its meaning, grammatical category, or both. Three parameters carve the construct: (1) position — the morpheme occurs after the stem, in contrast to prefixes (before the stem) and infixes (within the stem); (2) boundness — the suffix cannot occur as an independent word; it requires a host stem to be realized, making it grammatically dependent; (3) function — the suffix either derives a new lexical item (derivational suffix: noun-making -ness, adjective-making -ful) or marks a grammatical feature without changing category (inflectional suffix: plural -s, past tense -ed, comparative -er). Paradigmatic cases: English derivational suffix -ity (active → activity) and inflectional suffix -s (cat → cats); Latin -āre (infinitive marker); Turkish -lar (plural, agglutinative). Suffixes persist through morphological productivity — speakers apply suffix rules to new stems, and the inventory of suffixes is maintained in the grammatical descriptions and lexical entries of each language. [formal: suffixus | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

payload.body: A morpheme is the smallest unit of language that carries meaning or a grammatical function, and cannot be decomposed into smaller meaningful units. Three parameters carve the construct: (1) minimality - a morpheme is the shortest stretch of language that carries meaning or grammatical function on its own; the English word cats decomposes into the two morphemes cat and -s, and no smaller meaningful unit exists below that level; (2) the type-token distinction - a morpheme type is a repeatable unit that recurs across many tokens, and the inventory of types is finite in any given language; (3) the free-bound distinction - a morpheme is either free (it can stand as an independent word: house) or bound (it occurs only within a word: un-, -ness), and every word is composed of one or more morphemes. Paradigmatic cases: the English three-morpheme word unhappiness (un- + happy + -ness), the single-morpheme water, and the agglutinative Turkish evde (ev + de, in the house), where morpheme boundaries are maximally visible. The morpheme persists as a stable category of description: it is the basic unit of morphological analysis, stated in the grammars, textbooks and dictionaries of every language, and reproduced whenever a new word is analyzed. [formal: morphema | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

[formal: morphema | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

An affix is a bound morpheme that attaches to a host word stem (or base), modifying its meaning or grammatical function. Three parameters carve the construct: (1) boundness - an affix cannot occur as an independent word and is realized only inside a host word, which distinguishes affixes from free morphemes; (2) position - an affix is a prefix (before the stem, as in English un-), a suffix (after the stem, as in English -ness), or an infix (within the stem, as in Tagalog -um-), and the position is a fixed property of the affix in a given language; (3) function - an affix is either derivational (it produces a new lexical item, often of a different category: happy + -ness to happiness) or inflectional (it marks a grammatical feature within a paradigm: plural -s, past -ed). Paradigmatic cases: English -ness (adjective to noun), Latin -are (infinitive marker), Tagalog -um- (actor focus: kain to k-um-in). Affixes persist through morphological productivity - speakers apply affixation rules to new stems, and the inventory of affixes is maintained in the grammatical descriptions and lexical entries of each language. [formal: affixus | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Compounding is a word-formation process that combines two or more independent lexical items (free morphemes) into a single word. Three parameters carve the construct: (1) the components are free - each component is a word that can stand on its own, which distinguishes compounding from affixation (where the attached element is a bound morpheme) and from tmesis (where one independent element is inserted into the interior of a single host word); (2) the result is a single word - the components are juxtaposed and fused into one orthographic and prosodic unit; (3) compositionality - the meaning of a compound ranges from transparent (black + board, blackboard) to idiomatic (many + fold, manifold), and the degree of transparency is a parameter of each particular compound rather than of the process as a whole. Paradigmatic cases: English blackboard and skyscraper; German Haustuer (house + door); Japanese yamane (mountain + ape, monkey). Compounding persists as a productive rule of the grammar - speakers coin new compounds on the fly, and the inventory of compounds is maintained in dictionaries and lexical entries. [formal: compositio | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

payload.scope: Word formation is a human-made morphological category — the genus comprising the processes by which a language's speakers produce new words from existing lexical material — built to persist as the stable classification under which particular operations (compounding, affixation, infixation, tmesis) are catalogued in the grammars of the languages that use them.

payload.body: Word formation is the made category comprising the processes by which a language's speakers produce new words from existing lexical material. Three parameters carve the construct: (1) the input is existing lexical material of the language — stems, morphemes, or whole words — which separates word formation from borrowing (which introduces material from another language) and from one-off coinage by a single act of naming; (2) the output is a new word — a new lexical item entering the language's inventory, not a new phrase, sentence, or mere variant of an existing word; (3) the operations are rule-governed in a given language: each language has its own available operations and their combinations, so which formations are possible is a parameter of the grammar, not free invention. Its members include compounding (juxtaposing free morphemes into a single word), affixation (attaching bound morphemes to a stem), infixation (inserting a bound morpheme into a stem's interior), and tmesis (inserting a grammatically independent element into a word's interior); the board's entries for those operations are instances of this genus. Paradigmatic cases: English blackboard (compounding), English -ness (suffixation), Tagalog -um- (infixation: kain 'eat' to k-um-in), fan-frickin'-tastic (tmesis). Word formation persists as a category of grammatical description: its operations are catalogued in the grammars and dictionaries of each language, taught as a stable classification in linguistics, and applied productively by speakers who coin new words. [formal: formatio verborum | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

payload.body: Affixation is a morphological process in which a language attaches a bound morpheme — a prefix, suffix, or circumfix — to the edge of a word stem to produce a new word. Three parameters carve the construct: (1) the attached material is a bound morpheme, not an independent word, and it attaches at the stem's edge, not inside it, separating affixation from infixation and tmesis; (2) the host stem retains its lexical identity and the affixed form remains analyzable as stem plus affix; (3) the operation is rule-governed in a given language — which affixes exist, where they attach, and what meaning they contribute are parameters of the grammar, not free invention. Paradigmatic cases: English un-happy, cat-s, re-do; Arabic prefixation a-...; German circumfix ge-...-t. Affixation persists two ways: as a productive rule — speakers coin new affixed forms on the fly — and as a stable category of description — grammars, morphology textbooks, and formal rule specifications continue to state which affixes attach where and what they mark. [formal: affixatio | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

payload.body: Compounding is a word-formation process in which a language juxtaposes two or more free morphemes (independent words or lexical roots) into a single new word. Three parameters carve the construct: (1) the inputs are free morphemes — each retains its lexical identity and could function independently as a word in isolation; (2) the output is a single word, not a phrase: the compound exhibits phonological, syntactic, or morphological behavior as one unit (e.g., stress patterns, inflection on the final element only); (3) the semantic relationship between the constituents is governed by the grammar of the language — the compound does not simply mean the sum of its parts but establishes a conventionalized relationship (modification, possession, purpose, etc.). Paradigmatic cases: English blackboard (modifier-head), doghouse (purpose), swimwear (material-function). Compounding persists as a highly productive word-formation strategy across languages and as a stable category in lexical morphology and dictionary organization. [formal: compositio | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

payload.body: Morpheme is a human-made morphological category — the minimal meaningful unit of a language that cannot be further divided without losing or altering meaning. Three parameters carve the construct: (1) minimality: the unit cannot be decomposed into smaller meaningful parts within the language; (2) meaningfulness: the unit carries semantic, grammatical, or derivational content — it is not a mere phonological artifact; (3) language-relativity: what counts as a morpheme in one language may not align with morpheme boundaries in another, since the inventory of morphemes is a parameter of each language's grammar. Types include free morphemes (can stand alone as words, e.g. English 'book'), bound morphemes (must attach to other material, e.g. English '-s' plural, 'un-' negation), and allomorphs (phonologically varied forms of the same morpheme). Morphemes persist as the atom of morphological analysis: grammarians decompose words into morphemes, dictionaries catalog them, and speakers productively combine them according to the rules of their language. [formal: morphema | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

payload.body: Affix is a human-made morphological category — a bound morpheme that attaches to a word stem (the base) to modify its meaning or grammatical function. Three parameters carve the construct: (1) boundness: the affix cannot stand alone as an independent word, distinguishing it from free morphemes; (2) attachment position: the affix attaches at a specific edge of the stem — prefixation (before the stem), suffixation (after the stem), circumfixation (around both edges), or infixation (inside the stem), each position having distinct grammatical consequences; (3) function: the affix contributes either derivational content (creating a new lexeme, e.g. English -ness turning 'happy' into 'happiness') or inflectional content (marking grammatical relations without changing lexeme identity, e.g. English -s for plural). Types by position include prefixes (un-, re-), suffixes (-ness, -s), circumfixes (German ge-...-t), and infixes (Tagalog -um-). Affixes persist as a productive morphological resource: speakers attach them productively in their language, and grammars catalog them as part of the morpheme inventory. [formal: affixus | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

payload.body: Stem is a human-made morphological category — the base of a word to which affixes attach, and the residue left when affixes are removed. Three parameters carve the construct: (1) residuation: the stem is what remains of a word form once its affixes are taken away (walk in walks, walker); (2) attachability: the stem is the host material that affixation attaches to at the stem's edge and infixation inserts into the stem's interior — the operations name the stem as their host; (3) lexical status: a stem may be free (an independent word: dog in doghouse) or bound (a root that cannot stand alone in the language: struct- in construct, destruct). Stems persist as the unit of morphological analysis: grammarians decompose word forms into stem plus affix, dictionaries list the stem as the lemma, and speakers productively attach affixes to stems on the fly. [formal: caulis | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

payload.scope: A prefix is a type of affix — a bound morpheme that attaches to the beginning of a word stem to modify its meaning or grammatical function. Built to persist as a productive morphological resource across languages that employ prefixation.

payload.body: A prefix is a type of affix — a bound morpheme that attaches to the beginning of a word stem to modify its meaning or grammatical function. Two parameters carve the construct: (1) position: the affix attaches before the stem (e.g. English un- in unhappy, re- in rewrite), which distinguishes it from suffixes (after the stem), infixes (inside the stem), and circumfixes (around both edges); (2) function: the prefix contributes either derivational content (creating a new lexeme, e.g. un- happy → unhappy) or inflectional content (marking grammatical relations without changing lexeme identity, e.g. un- done as past participle). Prefixes persist as a productive morphological resource: speakers attach them productively in their language, and grammars catalog them as part of the affix inventory. [formal: prefixus | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

payload.body: A circumfix is a type of affix — a bound morpheme that attaches around both edges of a word stem simultaneously (prefixing and suffixing at once) to modify its meaning or grammatical function. Two parameters carve the construct: (1) position: the affix spans the stem with a prefixal element before it and a suffixal element after it, operating as a single unit (e.g. German ge-...-t in gedichtet 'founded' from dichten, Dutch be-...-en in bewerken 'to work on'), which distinguishes it from separate prefix and suffix attachments; (2) function: the circumfix contributes either derivational or inflectional content, but the key distinction from circumposition is that the two parts form a single bound morpheme that cannot be separated in the grammar. Circumfixes persist as a productive morphological resource in languages that employ them, and grammars catalog them as a distinct affix type. [formal: circumfixus | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

payload.body: An infix is a type of affix — a bound morpheme that attaches within the interior of a word stem to modify its meaning or grammatical function. Two parameters carve the construct: (1) position: the affix attaches inside the stem (e.g. Tagalog -um- in sumulat 'to write' from sulat, English 'abso-blooming-lutely'), which distinguishes it from prefixes (before the stem), suffixes (after the stem), and circumfixes (around both edges); (2) function: the infix contributes either derivational content (creating a new lexeme) or inflectional content (marking grammatical relations without changing lexeme identity). Infixed persist as a productive morphological resource: speakers attach them productively in languages that employ infixation, and grammars catalog them as part of the affix inventory. [formal: infixus | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

payload.scope: Root is a human-made morphological category — the core lexical unit of a word — built to persist as the atom of morphological and etymological analysis in grammars, dictionaries, and comparative linguistics.

payload.body: Root is a human-made morphological category — the core lexical unit of a word: the residue that remains once ALL affixes, derivational and inflectional alike, are removed. Three parameters carve the construct: (1) maximal residuation: the root is what remains when every affix is stripped, which separates it from the stem — the residue after removing inflectional affixes only, which may still carry derivational material (in 'nationalities' the root is nation and the stem is national; in 'disagreement' the root is agree and the stem is disagree; where no derivational material is present the two coincide, so in 'walks' root and stem are both walk); (2) free/bound duality: in some languages the root is a free morpheme standing alone as a word (walk in walks, walker), in others it is bound and cannot stand alone (struct- in construct, destruction, structure) — both cases fall inside the category, paralleling the stem's own free/bound distinction; (3) lexical core: the root carries the word's core lexical meaning — affixes contribute derivational or inflectional content, but the root is what survives decomposition as the meaning-bearer. Roots persist as the atom of morphological and etymological analysis: grammars decompose word forms into root plus affixes, dictionaries list the root as the lemma, and comparative and historical linguistics track one root across cognate languages (PIE *bʰer- 'to carry' in Latin ferre and English bear). [formal: radix | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

payload.note: Pinned sense (Law 11d): root as the core lexical unit of a word, free or bound. INSTANCE_OF test (Law 9): every root is a morpheme — a free morpheme when it stands alone as a word (walk in walks, walker), a bound morpheme when it cannot (struct- in construct, destruction) — and morpheme is the NEAREST accepted kind: the board's only accepted kind under morpheme is affix, and a root is not an affix (an affix attaches to a host stem to modify it; a root is the host material that affixes attach to, the residue that remains when they are removed). The morpheme definition's own type list (free morphemes, bound morphemes, allomorphs) covers every case of root. Specific-to-general: roots are the meaning-bearing core of the morpheme inventory, not the inventory. (Laws 9, 11d, 11e.)

Pinned sense (Law 11d): both as technical categories of morphological analysis. DERIVED_FROM test (Law 7) — which came first, from independent historical reasoning, not the graph's epoch: the ROOT concept is the older category, attested in the oldest grammatical traditions (Sanskrit dhatu 'verbal root' in Panini, 4th c. BCE; Semitic triconsonantal roots as the classic paradigm; 'etymological root' in Indo-European historical linguistics). The technical STEM category — the unit to which inflection attaches, distinct from the etymological core — crystallized in 19th-century comparative morphology, when the older root/base idea was split into Wurzel (etymological root) and Stamm (inflectional stem). The stem concept was carved out of the root concept by peeling off derivational material; the reverse history is not available. Ordering rests on the history of grammatical literature, not on the graph's epoch estimate (Law 7 anti-circularity).

The pinned sense (Law 11d) fails the target's accepted definition. Affixation's standing definition makes edge-attachment constitutive: parameter (1) says the morpheme 'attaches at the stem's edge, not inside it, separating affixation from infixation and tmesis' — the genus names infixation as what it is NOT. 'Same operation, different placement' cannot make interior insertion an instance of a category whose first parameter excludes it. And the board already seats the true relation: infixation INST word-formation and affixation INST word-formation are both ACCEPTED — infixation and affixation are SIBLING processes under word-formation, not parent and child. Filing against affixation would also make the edge derivable through the accepted sibling ladder.

Remove the concept of stem and the type loses its relational anchor: a position label with nothing to wrap. Circumfix is the third position-specific type defined relative to a stem, so the same constitutive dependency holds.

The removal test fails. Prefix's standing definition operates entirely on {bound morpheme, word stem, position}: 'a bound morpheme that attaches to the beginning of a word stem'. Nowhere does the affixation concept need to be invoked — the morphologist identifying un- in un-happy as a prefix does a static decomposition (bound morpheme, located before the stem), not an appeal to the derivation process. 'Without the process, the type has nothing to do' is an unsupported constitutive assertion (Laws 8/8b): a type does not depend on the process that names it. The genuine dependency runs the other way and the board already seats it: affixation DEP affix [ACCEPTED] and affixation DEP stem [ACCEPTED] — the process depends on its material and host, not vice versa. Prefix is an INSTANCE of affix (prefix INST affix, ACCEPTED), not a dependent of affixation.

payload.note: Infixation is the process of inserting an infix (a type of affix) into the interior of a word stem. Removal test (Laws 8/8b): remove infix — the bound morpheme that infixation inserts — and the process loses its operational target. Infixation operates on infixes; without them, there is nothing to insert. Constitutive dependency.

Prefix is a type of affix that attaches to the beginning of a word stem. Removal test (Laws 8/8b): remove the concept of stem — the base unit the prefix wraps — and prefix loses its operational meaning. A prefix is defined by its attachment to a stem; without stem, the prefix is an unanchored bound morpheme with no structural position. Constitutive dependency.

payload.body: Word form is a human-made morphological category — the particular inflected or derived shape a word takes in a language (walks, walked, walking; the plural cat-s, the past un-done), distinguished from the abstract word by its place in the inflectional and derivational system. Three parameters carve the construct: (1) SURFACE PARTICULARITY — a word form is a concrete shape in use or citation, not an abstract lexical item: 'walks' and 'walked' are distinct word forms of the one word 'walk', which subsumes them as its inventory of shapes; (2) DECOMPOSABILITY — a word form is analyzable into morphological parts, stem plus affix (walk + -s, un + do + -e), or stands whole as a one-morpheme form (dog, which is its own stem) — decomposition is the operation the category is made for, and a form's being decomposable is what makes its stem and its affixes locatable; (3) PARADIGMATIC PLACEMENT — a word form occupies a defined cell in a paradigm (the 3rd-person singular present cell of walk), so a word's forms constitute a finite, predictable inventory in a given language rather than an open set of arbitrary shapes. Word forms persist as the unit of lexicographic and morphological analysis: dictionaries paradigmize them (conjugation tables, inflection tables, headword listings), grammarians decompose them into stem plus affix, and speakers produce them on the fly under the rules of their language. [formal: forma verbi | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

This cadence is specifically about chord successions in tonal music that create points of arrival (authentic), pause (half), evasion (deceptive), or solemn closure (plagal) — a musical construct, not a general process of ending or concluding.

payload.body: Cadence is a human-made musical construct — a patterned sequence of harmonic and melodic motions that marks a point of rest, pause, or continuation in tonal music. Three parameters carve the construct: (1) harmonic progression — a cadence consists of a specific succession of chords (e.g., dominant to tonic in authentic cadences, subdominant to tonic in plagal cadences, or tonic to dominant in half cadences); (2) cadential function — it serves one of three structural roles: termination (a final rest, as in a perfect authentic cadence), interruption/pause (a temporary halt that invites continuation, as in a half cadence), or evasion/subversion (an expected resolution that avoids closure, as in a deceptive cadence where dominant resolves to submediant instead of tonic); (3) metric placement — the cadence occurs at a metrically salient point, typically a strong beat or downbeat, which gives it perceptual weight as a structural landmark. Cadences persist through their codification in Western tonal theory: they are named and classified in harmony textbooks (perfect authentic, imperfect authentic, plagal, half, deceptive, and their variants), taught in music-theory curricula as essential markers of phrase and period boundaries, reproduced in composition as the structural punctuation of musical discourse, and perceived by listeners as points of arrival, pause, or expectation. Distinctions: from a single chord (a cadence is a multi-chord progression, never a single harmony); from a bare resolution (the specific chord succession and its metric placement are constitutive, not the mere fact of stability); from a phrase (a cadence is the terminal motion of a phrase or section, not the phrase itself). [formal: cadentia | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Pinned sense (Law 11d) is identity: 'The infix IS a morpheme — a bound meaningful element.' Law 8c: identity is not dependency — the filer's own words describe an INSTANCE_OF relation, not a DEPENDS_ON one. The removal test fails as sayability (Laws 2b/8b): the concept of infix operates without the concept of morpheme; a bound element inserted inside a base can be described, catalogued, and used whether or not 'morpheme' is named. The note's nearest-kind claim — 'no intermediate kind stands between infix and morpheme on the board' — is refuted by the accepted affix entry (ee47455a), whose accepted definition lists infixation as a position type, and by the accepted infix INSTANCE_OF affix edge g18f2e87 filed by the filer himself 25 hours before this one. The kind relation this note actually describes is already on the board: infix -> affix -> morpheme, all accepted. The board's accepted DEPENDS_ON pattern into morpheme is process->manipulated object (affixation, compounding, infixation — processes that manipulate morphemes); an infix is a kind of morpheme, not a process that manipulates one. Accepting this would double-record an already-accepted kind relation under the wrong type and corrupt the removal-test semantics of DEPENDS_ON. STRIKE.
